title: Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2015
short_title: Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2015

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would force telecommunications companies to keep certain data for law enforcement and national security purposes.
It sets standard types of data to retain and a minimum retention period, and restricts which agencies can access the data.
The Commonwealth Ombudsman would oversee compliance, and the scheme must be reviewed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security within three years of starting.
changes: Standardises the kinds of telecommunications data that service providers must keep.
Limits which agencies are allowed to access telecommunications data as a 'criminal law enforcement agency'.
Introduces oversight by the Commonwealth Ombudsman of enforcement agencies' access to data.
Restricts stored communications warrants to interception agencies and other law enforcement bodies with a demonstrated need.
summary.affected: Telecommunications service providers, law enforcement agencies, and national security agencies are affected.

This amendment is designed to ensure that access to privacy-intrusive telecommunications data is permitted only for serious crimes. The bill was clearly intended with a national security remit: serious crimes. Any extension beyond terrorism and national security should only be to crimes that are in the upper range of seriousness in all Australian jurisdictions, such as child pornography offences. I do not wish to see metadata used to pursue trivialities. That is what happened in the UK, with the RIPA law. This is probably the most important amendment that the Australian Greens will move during this debate. It is colloquially known as the get-a-warrant amendment. We strongly believe that in 1979 when this act was passed into law that if we had had the multitude of devices, data types and platforms that we have today, the drafters who were considering the substantial overall of telecommunications interception legislation as they were in 1979 would have looked around the field and said, 'You can tap people's phone, you can read people's email, you can track their movements around the landscape, and you can map of their social networks and find everything about their lives. These things will all be covered by a warrant and what will not be covered by a warrant is simple subscriber data so that agencies can very rapidly establish who owns the handset, who holds a particular prescription for a particular service. And so we would have ended up with the same two-tiered system that we have today, but those invasive forms of data access—whether they be tapping the phone call or reading your location as you move around the place—would have been within the warranted regime. I have no doubt about that at all. What we have seen, quite frankly, is the failure of the law to keep up with the march of technology. We still have a fairly robust warranted regime. This division was for whether or not to accept [Nick Xenophon’s](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/nick_xenophon) motion to amend the [Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2015](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5375). [Xenophon summarised the amendment in Parliament](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2015-03-26.236.1): > This amendment addresses issues relating to disclosures of information by journalists, through amendments to the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Act 1979, the Crimes Act 1914 and the Criminal Code Act 1995. These amendments address changes to these acts made by the previous bills in this tranche of legislation, primarily the National Security Legislation Amendment Act (No. 1) 2014. > > Make no mistake about it, these issues go to the heart of press freedom in this country in relation to the ability of investigative journalists to do their work. These bills insert into these acts new offences relating to the disclosure of information relating to a special intelligence operation, as well as for publishing advertisements or items of news that contain information about recruitment of people to armed forces in a foreign country. I want to make it clear that, in relation to any publication of information in respect of a special intelligence operation that could endanger the lives of those involved in the operation or other lives directly as a result of that disclosure of information, I do not oppose the imposition of a penalty. If we are talking about endangering lives—if, for instance, there is an ASIS or ASIO officer whose life is put in real danger by the disclosure of their identity—then that is a serious matter. speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 after securing amendments including mandatory data breach notification, encryption, a warrant regime for journalists’ data, dataset defined in legislation, and expanded oversight by the Ombudsman and Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security. Labor also committed to introducing reforms for stronger parliamentary oversight of intelligence and security agencies.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Nikolic
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 is vital for national security, citing that metadata is used in 100% of cybercrime investigations, 90% of counterterrorism and child protection cases, and 80% of serious organised crime investigations. The bill would reduce agencies with metadata access from around 80 to about 20, provide oversight by the Ombudsman, Privacy Commissioner, and Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security, and the government would cover reasonable upfront costs, estimated at less than 1% of the telecommunications sector's revenue.

speeches.speaker: Jason Clare
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the original Data Retention Bill gave too much power to the Attorney-General and lacked privacy protections, and supported 38 committee amendments including embedding metadata definitions in legislation, requiring warrants for journalists' data, and providing oversight resources. They noted that major telcos Telstra, Optus and Vodafone have no current plans to reduce data retention, and that the bill’s main effect would be consistency rather than preventing a "going dark" scenario.

speeches.speaker: Philip Ruddock
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 is essential for national security, claiming that existing metadata access is inadequate and that commercial interests are undermining data retention. He cited threats from terrorism and organised crime, referenced half a million metadata requests, and criticised media and tech firms like Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales for opposing the bill on privacy grounds.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The speaker criticised the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014, noting that Minister Malcolm Turnbull had changed his stance from opposing data retention in opposition to introducing the bill in government. The speaker detailed 38 unanimous recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, including specifying the data set in legislation, limiting access to listed law enforcement agencies, prohibiting use for civil litigation, and requiring encryption and a mandatory data breach notification scheme.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Data Retention Bill is necessary to address gaps in law enforcement's ability to investigate serious crimes like child exploitation and terrorism, as changing technology has reduced data availability. The bill requires telecommunications providers to retain metadata for two years, excludes content like web browsing history and passwords, and includes 39 bipartisan recommendations to limit access to around 20 agencies, with government support for cost contributions and oversight.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: The speaker criticised the government's rushed and politically motivated process for introducing the data retention bill, arguing it bypassed proper community engagement. They noted that Labor's amendments placed the datasets in legislation, limited the number of authorised agencies from over 80 to 20, gave consumers access to their metadata, restricted use for civil proceedings, and required data-breach notifications.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014, as amended by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security’s 38 recommendations, strikes a necessary balance by standardising metadata retention, limiting access to 12 listed agencies (down from over 80), requiring encryption and mandatory data breach notifications, and adding oversight by the Commonwealth Ombudsman and PJCIS, while also requiring a warrant for journalists’ metadata.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Henderson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 is a key anti-terrorism measure, noting that over 25 countries have similar laws and that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security made 39 unanimous recommendations on the bill. He criticised the member for Perth for undermining bipartisan support, cited recent terrorist attacks (Martin Place siege, Charlie Hebdo, Copenhagen shootings, Endeavour Hills attack), and stated that ASIO is investigating roughly 400 high-priority cases.

speeches.speaker: Sarah Henderson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the data retention bill is vital for security, citing that metadata was used in 92% of counter-terrorism investigations, and announced the bill requires ISPs to retain metadata for two years with safeguards including a warrant for journalist metadata.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the current system allows over half a million warrantless telecommunications data accesses annually by a wide range of agencies including the RSPCA, and that the amended bill introduces safeguards such as a defined dataset, restricted agency access, a warrant requirement for journalists' data, encryption, customer access rights, and a mandatory review within four years.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 is a bad law that treats all Australians as suspects, requires no warrant for metadata access, and will only catch unsophisticated criminals while infringing on privacy. They moved an amendment to delay the bill until a review addresses civil litigants' access to data, data destruction requirements, and impacts on journalism.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the data retention bill, while improved by amendments, remains flawed, citing concerns over costs (estimated at $189–319 million), the two-year retention period, and journalist protections, and stressed the need for ongoing parliamentary oversight.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wilkie
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the mandatory two-year metadata retention bill, arguing it was an unprecedented extension of state power and a step toward a police state, noting that security agencies accessed metadata 290,358 times in 2011-12 and 319,874 times in 2012-13 without warrants, and called for warrant requirements and stronger parliamentary oversight.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The bill standardises metadata retention by requiring telecommunications companies and internet service providers to retain specified classes of metadata for two years, without granting new powers to access metadata or expanding the types of data accessible. The government supports all 39 recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, including specifying the dataset and agencies in primary legislation and increasing oversight and privacy protections.

speeches.speaker: Melissa Parke
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the mandatory data retention bill poses serious risks to privacy, media freedom, and free expression, noting that over 80 agencies can already access metadata without a warrant, and that the bill lacks adequate safeguards, proportionality, and evidence of necessity—despite some improvements from committee amendments, significant concerns remain about cost ($400 million), security, oversight, and the potential for misuse against whistleblowers and journalists.

speeches.speaker: Luke Simpkins
speeches.brief: The speaker endorsed the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014, arguing that mandatory two-year metadata retention is essential for investigating terrorism, child exploitation and organised crime, and noted the bill introduces new warrant protections for journalists' metadata. He also proposed making it a criminal offence to share or retweet social media posts from prescribed terrorist organisations such as Daesh, al-Nusra or Hamas.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 subject to amendments, including onshore data storage, government funding, journalist and whistleblower protections, and prohibiting civil litigation use, noting that over half a million metadata access applications were made in the previous year under an unregulated system.

speeches.speaker: Dan Tehan
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for passing the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014, stating it would require telecom providers to retain metadata for two years without web-browsing history or content, and included 38 committee recommendations to strengthen oversight and safeguards, such as additional funding for the Commonwealth Ombudsman and a warrant requirement for accessing journalist source data. He cited national security threats, including 90 Australians fighting in Iraq and Syria and 30 returned, and the use of metadata in the Operation Pendennis terrorism investigation.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: The speaker criticised the government's handling of the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014, arguing it was initially "shambolic and unpassable" and required Labor's insistence for proper review and 38 committee recommendations to become supportable. They noted warrantless data accesses rose from 330,000 in 2012-13 to 500,000 in 2013-14, and credited Labor's push for improved regulation, including applying the Privacy Act, requiring encrypted storage, limiting warrantless access to a narrower set of agencies, increasing Ombudsman oversight, and securing journalist protections from the Prime Minister.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: The member argued the bill does not expand law enforcement access to metadata, does not allow warrantless phone tapping or email reading, and excludes web browsing history, while mandating two-year retention of existing metadata types. The bill has bipartisan support following a committee report with 39 recommendations.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014, which mandates that telecommunications providers retain metadata for two years to assist law enforcement and national security agencies, while explicitly excluding content and internet browsing, and includes oversight by the Commonwealth Ombudsman and a parliamentary review after three years.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014, arguing it regulates the current unregulated access to metadata—over 500,000 applications annually by 80+ agencies—and balances security with rights. Key amendments secured by Labor include requiring a warrant for accessing journalists' metadata, mandating onshore data storage, encryption, a data breach notification scheme, and expanded parliamentary oversight.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that metadata is not content and is essential for investigating serious crime, noting that 85-90% of recent serious crime and terrorism investigations used metadata, and that the bill reduces the number of bodies with access from 80 to 20. They asserted that the legislation includes parliamentary oversight, protects privacy proportionally, and does not limit press freedom or compromise legal privilege.
